# Goal and overview

This notebook gets the NHANES 2021–2023 dataset (dataset 3) ready for analysis. Following the
guiding questions of Part 1, we:

1. describe the structure of the data and the type of every variable;
2. recode NHANES special codes ("refused", "don't know", "indeterminate") to missing values;
3. remove redundant and uninformative columns (unit duplicates, constant columns, analytes that are mostly below the detection limit);
4. map where values are missing and *why* they are missing;
5. define the analysis population and filter features;
6. look for implausible values and outlying participants;
7. transform skewed variables;
8. check with correlation heatmaps and PCA whether participants cluster by biology or by technical factors;
9. export the preprocessed dataset together with a variable dictionary and a log of every decision.

Every decision is stored in `preprocessing_log`, which is exported at the end so it can be cited in the
methods section of the report.

Useful NHANES documentation (variable definitions and special codes):

* Demographics: <https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/search/datapage.aspx?Component=Demographics&Cycle=2021-2023>
* Laboratory: <https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/search/datapage.aspx?Component=Laboratory&Cycle=2021-2023>
* Example of a variable page (`RIDSTATR`): <https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2021/DataFiles/DEMO_L.htm#RIDSTATR>

## Libraries and parameters

All thresholds are defined once here, so that a different choice can be tested by changing one line.

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(ComplexHeatmap)
library(circlize)
library(RColorBrewer)

set.seed(2026)

# folder that contains the two csv files
data_dir <- "."
data_file     <- file.path(data_dir, "NHANES_20212023_merged_filtered_1.csv")
codebook_file <- file.path(data_dir, "NHANES_20212023_codebook_filtered_1.csv")

# preprocessing parameters (justified in the corresponding sections)
MIN_AGE             <- 20    # analysis population: adults aged 20+ (education is only asked from 20 on)
MAX_MISSING_FEATURE <- 0.50  # drop features missing in > 50% of the analysis population
MAX_BELOW_LOD       <- 0.50  # drop analytes with > 50% of the values below the detection limit
NZV_THRESHOLD       <- 0.95  # drop features where one value makes up > 95% of the observations
SKEW_THRESHOLD      <- 1     # log2-transform continuous features with skewness > 1
ROBUST_Z            <- 5     # flag values more than 5 robust SDs from the median (after transformation)
PCA_MAX_MISSING     <- 0.20  # lab features used for PCA may be missing in at most 20% of participants

# helper to log every preprocessing decision
preprocessing_log <- tibble(step = character(), n_samples = integer(),
                            n_features = integer(), decision = character())
log_step <- function(step, data, decision) {
  preprocessing_log <<- add_row(preprocessing_log, step = step, n_samples = nrow(data),
                                n_features = ncol(data), decision = decision)
}

# skewness without extra packages
skewness <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (length(x) < 3 || sd(x) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3
}
```

# Reading the data

```{r read}
nhanes_raw <- read_csv(data_file, guess_max = 12000)

# the codebook contains a few non-UTF8 characters (e.g. µ), hence the latin1 encoding
codebook <- read_csv(codebook_file, locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")) %>%
  mutate(cb_index = row_number())

dim(nhanes_raw)
nhanes_raw[1:5, 1:8]

# every column should be documented in the codebook
setdiff(names(nhanes_raw), codebook$variable)
length(unique(nhanes_raw$SEQN)) == nrow(nhanes_raw)   # one row per participant?

log_step("Raw data", nhanes_raw, "Merged NHANES 2021-2023 file as provided (one row per participant, SEQN unique).")
```

The raw table contains **`r nrow(nhanes_raw)` participants** (rows) and **`r ncol(nhanes_raw)` variables**
(columns), coming from `r n_distinct(codebook$file)` NHANES data files in four components.

```{r components}
codebook %>%
  count(component, file, name = "n_variables") %>%
  group_by(component) %>%
  summarise(n_files = n(), n_variables = sum(n_variables)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Number of NHANES data files and variables per component")
```

# Variable types

Most NHANES columns are stored as numbers, also when they are categories (e.g. `RIAGENDR`: 1 = male,
2 = female). Treating such codes as measurements would be wrong, so we first assign every variable a
**role** and a **type**. The categorical variables were classified by hand using the NHANES documentation;
the remaining numeric variables are measurements.

```{r variable-types}
weights_design <- c("SDDSRVYR", "SDMVSTRA", "SDMVPSU", grep("^WT", names(nhanes_raw), value = TRUE))

technical <- c("RIDSTATR",            # interviewed only (1) or interviewed + examined (2)
               "RIDEXMON",            # six-month period of the exam (Nov-Apr / May-Oct)
               "PHDSESNZ",            # exam session (morning / afternoon-evening)
               "BMDSTATS",            # body measures status code
               "BPAOARM", "BPAOCSZ",  # arm and cuff size used for blood pressure
               grep("^BMI(WT|RECUM|HEAD|HT|LEG|ARML|ARMC|WAIST|HIP)$", names(nhanes_raw), value = TRUE),
               grep("^PH(Q|A)", names(nhanes_raw), value = TRUE))   # fasting questionnaire

# limit-of-detection comment codes (0 = at/above, 1 = below detection limit)
lod_codes <- codebook %>%
  filter(component == "Laboratory",
         str_detect(label, regex("comment|cmt|comt", ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%
  pull(variable)

nominal <- c("RIAGENDR", "RIDRETH1", "RIDRETH3", "DMQMILIZ", "DMDBORN4", "DMDMARTZ", "RIDEXPRG",
             "DMDHRGND", "DMDHRMAZ", "LBXHA", "LBXHBS", "LBXHBC", "LBDHBG", "LBDHD", "LBXHCR",
             "LBDHCI", "LBXHCG", "LBDHEG", "LBDHEM", "URXPREG", "ALQ111", "ALQ151", "DBQ010",
             grep("^DBQ073", names(nhanes_raw), value = TRUE),
             "DBQ301", "DBQ330", "DBQ360", "DBQ370", "DBQ390", "DBQ400", "DBQ421", "DBQ424",
             "DBQ930", "DBQ935", "DBQ940", "DBQ945", "ECQ080", "ECQ090", "WHQ030E", "MCQ080E")

ordinal  <- c("DMDYRUSR", "DMDEDUC2", "DMDHRAGZ", "DMDHREDZ", "DMDHSEDZ", "BMDBMIC",
              "ALQ121", "ALQ142", "ALQ270", "ALQ280")        # ALQ1xx/2xx: frequency categories 0-10

discrete <- c("RIDAGEYR", "RIDAGEMN", "RIDEXAGM", "DMDHHSIZ", "ALQ130", "ALQ170",
              "DBD030", "DBD041", "DBD050", "DBD055", "DBD061", "DBD381", "DBD411",
              "ECD070A", "ECD070B")

variable_overview <- codebook %>%
  filter(variable %in% names(nhanes_raw)) %>%
  mutate(type = case_when(
    variable == "SEQN"              ~ "identifier",
    variable %in% weights_design    ~ "survey weight / design",
    variable %in% technical         ~ "technical / status",
    variable %in% lod_codes         ~ "detection-limit flag",
    variable %in% nominal           ~ "nominal",
    variable %in% ordinal           ~ "ordinal",
    variable %in% discrete          ~ "discrete",
    TRUE                            ~ "continuous"))

variable_overview %>%
  count(component, type) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = component, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Variable roles and types per component")
```

```{r variable-types-plot, fig.height = 4}
variable_overview %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_rev(fct_infreq(type)), fill = component)) +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.line.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "", y = "number of variables", fill = "NHANES component",
       title = "Most variables are continuous laboratory measurements")
```

**Observations.** The laboratory component dominates the dataset. About a quarter of the columns are not
biological features at all: survey weights and design variables, technical status variables and
detection-limit flags. These are kept as metadata (weights, technical factors) or used for quality
control (detection-limit flags), but are not analysed as features.

# Special codes

NHANES stores answers such as "refused" (7, 77, 777, ...) and "don't know" (9, 99, 999, ...) as numbers
in the same column as the real answers. Left in, a "don't know" on the number of drinks per day
(`ALQ130` = 999) would be read as 999 drinks. A blanket replacement of every 7 or 9 is **not** an option,
because for continuous variables these are valid values. We therefore list the codes per variable, as
documented on the NHANES variable pages.

```{r special-codes}
special_codes <- list(
  # demographics
  DMQMILIZ = c(7, 9), DMDYRUSR = c(77, 99), DMDEDUC2 = c(7, 9), DMDMARTZ = c(77, 99),
  DMDBORN4 = c(77, 99), DMDHREDZ = c(7, 9), DMDHRMAZ = c(77, 99), DMDHSEDZ = c(7, 9),
  RIDEXPRG = 3,                                   # "cannot ascertain"
  # alcohol questionnaire
  ALQ111 = c(7, 9), ALQ121 = c(77, 99), ALQ130 = c(777, 999), ALQ142 = c(77, 99),
  ALQ270 = c(77, 99), ALQ280 = c(77, 99), ALQ151 = c(7, 9), ALQ170 = c(777, 999),
  # diet behaviour (children) and early childhood
  DBQ010 = c(7, 9), DBQ073A = c(77, 99), DBQ073B = c(77, 99), DBQ073C = c(77, 99),
  DBQ073D = c(77, 99), DBQ073E = c(77, 99), DBQ073U = c(77, 99),
  DBQ301 = c(7, 9), DBQ330 = c(7, 9), DBQ360 = c(7, 9), DBQ370 = c(7, 9), DBQ390 = c(7, 9),
  DBQ400 = c(7, 9), DBQ421 = c(7, 9), DBQ424 = c(7, 9), DBQ930 = c(7, 9), DBQ935 = c(7, 9),
  DBQ940 = c(7, 9), DBQ945 = c(7, 9),
  # 666666 = "still breastfeeding / never fed ...": not a number of days
  DBD030 = c(666666, 777777, 999999), DBD041 = c(666666, 777777, 999999),
  DBD050 = c(666666, 777777, 999999), DBD055 = c(666666, 777777, 999999),
  DBD061 = c(666666, 777777, 999999), DBD381 = c(7777, 9999), DBD411 = c(7777, 9999),
  ECD070A = c(7777, 9999), ECD070B = c(7777, 9999), ECQ080 = c(7, 9), ECQ090 = c(7, 9),
  WHQ030E = c(7, 9), MCQ080E = c(7, 9),
  # laboratory: "indeterminate" test results
  LBXHA = 3, LBXHBC = 3, LBDHEG = 3, URXPREG = 3
)

n_recoded <- map_int(names(special_codes), ~ sum(nhanes_raw[[.x]] %in% special_codes[[.x]]))
tibble(variable = names(special_codes), n_recoded = n_recoded) %>%
  filter(n_recoded > 0) %>%
  left_join(codebook %>% select(variable, label), by = "variable") %>%
  arrange(desc(n_recoded)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Number of special codes recoded to NA per variable")

nhanes <- nhanes_raw
for (v in names(special_codes)) {
  nhanes[[v]][nhanes[[v]] %in% special_codes[[v]]] <- NA
}
log_step("Special codes", nhanes,
         paste0("Recoded ", sum(n_recoded), " refused/don't know/indeterminate codes to NA (variable-specific code lists)."))
```

## Skip patterns: "not asked" is not "missing"

Questionnaires use skip patterns: participants who never drank alcohol (`ALQ111` = 2) are not asked how often they
drank in the past year, and participants who did not drink in the past year (`ALQ121` = 0) are not asked how many
drinks they had. These values are empty in the data, but their true value is known: zero. Treating them as missing
would throw away about a fifth of the adults and, worse, mainly the non-drinkers.

```{r skip-patterns}
missing_before <- colSums(is.na(nhanes[nhanes$RIDAGEYR >= 18, c("ALQ121", "ALQ130", "ALQ142", "ALQ151")]))

nhanes <- nhanes %>%
  mutate(ALQ121 = if_else(ALQ111 %in% 2 & is.na(ALQ121), 0, ALQ121),     # never drank -> not in past year
         ALQ151 = if_else(ALQ111 %in% 2 & is.na(ALQ151), 2, ALQ151),     # never drank -> "no"
         ALQ130 = if_else(ALQ121 %in% 0 & is.na(ALQ130), 0, ALQ130),     # no drinks in past year -> 0 per day
         ALQ142 = if_else(ALQ121 %in% 0 & is.na(ALQ142), 0, ALQ142))     # -> never 4/5+ drinks

missing_after <- colSums(is.na(nhanes[nhanes$RIDAGEYR >= 18, c("ALQ121", "ALQ130", "ALQ142", "ALQ151")]))
rbind(missing_before, missing_after)

log_step("Skip patterns", nhanes,
         "Filled skipped alcohol questions with their implied value (0 drinks / 'no') for never or past-year non-drinkers.")
```

The remaining missing values in the alcohol questions are mostly participants who were not examined (the
alcohol questionnaire is completed in the examination centre) and a few who did not complete it.

As a safety net, we list non-laboratory numeric variables whose maximum still looks like a code:

```{r special-codes-check}
variable_overview %>%
  filter(type %in% c("nominal", "ordinal", "discrete"), variable %in% names(nhanes)) %>%
  mutate(max_value = map_dbl(variable, ~ suppressWarnings(max(nhanes[[.x]], na.rm = TRUE)))) %>%
  filter(max_value %in% c(7, 9, 77, 99, 777, 999, 7777, 9999, 77777, 99999)) %>%
  select(variable, label, max_value)
```

The remaining hits are valid values (e.g. a frequency category of 9, or a household of 7 people), which we
verified in the documentation. Note also that some variables are **top-coded**: `RIDAGEYR` = 80 means
"80 years or older", `INDFMPIR` = 5 means "income at least 5 times the poverty line", and `DMDHHSIZ` = 7
means "7 or more people". These values are kept, but the ceiling should be kept in mind when modelling.

The effect of the recoding on a questionnaire variable:

```{r special-codes-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
bind_rows(
  tibble(value = nhanes_raw$ALQ130, version = "before recoding"),
  tibble(value = nhanes$ALQ130,     version = "after recoding")) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(version = fct_relevel(version, "before recoding")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~version, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "average number of alcoholic drinks per day (ALQ130)", y = "number of participants")
```

# Redundant and uninformative columns

## Duplicated units

Many laboratory results are reported twice: in conventional units (e.g. mg/dL) and in SI units
(e.g. mmol/L). Both columns carry the same information. They are detected as variables from the same
data file whose label is identical apart from the unit between brackets; the first (conventional) unit is
kept.

```{r unit-duplicates}
unit_duplicates <- variable_overview %>%
  filter(type %in% c("continuous", "discrete")) %>%
  mutate(stem = str_squish(str_remove(label, "\\s*\\([^()]*\\)\\s*$"))) %>%
  group_by(file, stem) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  mutate(keep = row_number() == 1) %>%
  ungroup()

unit_duplicates %>%
  group_by(file, stem) %>%
  summarise(kept = variable[keep], removed = paste(variable[!keep], collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Unit duplicates: the conventional unit is kept")

# sanity check: kept and removed columns should be (almost) perfectly correlated
unit_duplicates %>%
  group_by(file, stem) %>%
  summarise(r = cor(nhanes[[variable[1]]], nhanes[[variable[2]]], use = "complete.obs"),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  summarise(min_correlation = min(r))

dup_unit_vars <- unit_duplicates %>% filter(!keep) %>% pull(variable)
```

All removed columns correlate (almost) perfectly with the kept column. The lowest correlation (≈ 0.96) is
for total calcium, where the SI values are rounded to two decimals; the information is the same. Three LDL estimates (Friedewald, Martin-Hopkins, NIH equation) are *not* unit duplicates:
they are different formulas and are kept for now.

## Detection limits

For many analytes (metals, PFAS, volatile organic compounds, hormones) a comment code indicates whether the
value is below the limit of detection (LOD). NHANES replaces such values by LOD/√2, so an analyte that is
mostly below the LOD is close to a constant and carries little information. Each comment code is linked to
its analyte (the nearest preceding measurement in the same data file) and the fraction of values below the
LOD is calculated.

```{r lod}
cb_measurements <- variable_overview %>%
  filter(!variable %in% c(lod_codes, dup_unit_vars, weights_design, technical))

lod_summary <- variable_overview %>%
  filter(variable %in% lod_codes) %>%
  select(lod_code = variable, file, cb_index) %>%
  mutate(analyte = map2_chr(file, cb_index, function(f, i) {
    cb_measurements %>% filter(file == f, cb_index < i) %>% slice_max(cb_index, n = 1) %>% pull(variable)
  })) %>%
  mutate(n_measured  = map_int(lod_code, ~ sum(!is.na(nhanes[[.x]]))),
         below_lod   = map_dbl(lod_code, ~ mean(nhanes[[.x]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  left_join(variable_overview %>% select(analyte = variable, label), by = "analyte")

# the mapping can be checked by eye
lod_summary %>% select(lod_code, analyte, label) %>% head(10)
```

```{r lod-plot, fig.height = 9}
lod_summary %>%
  filter(below_lod > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(paste0(analyte, " - ", str_trunc(label, 35)), below_lod),
             y = below_lod * 100, fill = below_lod > MAX_BELOW_LOD)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = MAX_BELOW_LOD * 100, linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey60", "#C95C4F"), labels = c("kept", "removed")) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6), axis.line.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "", y = "% of measured values below the limit of detection", fill = "",
       title = "Analytes with at least one value below the detection limit")
```

```{r lod-remove}
lod_removed <- lod_summary %>% filter(below_lod > MAX_BELOW_LOD) %>% pull(analyte)
length(lod_removed)
```

Analytes with more than `r MAX_BELOW_LOD * 100`% of their values below the detection limit are removed
(`r length(lod_removed)` analytes, mainly volatile organic compounds, several PFAS, ethyl/inorganic mercury
and minor folate forms). For the analytes that are kept, values below the LOD stay as provided (LOD/√2).
The comment codes themselves are not used as features.

## Constant columns, design variables and replicate readings

```{r constant}
constant_vars <- names(nhanes)[map_lgl(nhanes, ~ n_distinct(na.omit(.x)) <= 1)]
constant_vars
```

* **Constant columns** (`r length(constant_vars)`) carry no information, e.g. `SDDSRVYR` (same release
  cycle for everybody) and `LBDHD` (hepatitis D antibody, negative for everybody tested).
* **Survey weights and design variables** (`WT...`, `SDMVPSU`, `SDMVSTRA`) are not features. NHANES
  oversamples some groups; population estimates would require a weighted (survey) analysis with
  `WTMEC2YR`, `SDMVPSU` and `SDMVSTRA`. We keep these columns as metadata so this remains possible, but
  analyse the data unweighted, which is acceptable for the association analyses in Parts 2–4 (and is
  mentioned as a limitation).
* **Blood pressure** was measured three times (technical replicates). We use the mean of the available
  readings, as is common practice. The plot below shows that the readings agree well, with the first
  reading slightly higher on average (a known "white coat" effect, and a reason to average).

```{r bp-readings, fig.height = 3.5}
nhanes %>%
  select(SEQN, BPXOSY1, BPXOSY2, BPXOSY3) %>%
  pivot_longer(-SEQN, names_to = "reading", values_to = "systolic") %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  group_by(SEQN) %>%
  mutate(diff_from_mean = systolic - mean(systolic)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(reading = str_replace(reading, "BPXOSY", "reading ")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reading, y = diff_from_mean)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.3, fill = "grey85") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.line.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "", y = "difference from participant's mean (mmHg)",
       title = "Systolic blood pressure: agreement between the three readings")
```

```{r derived}
nhanes <- nhanes %>%
  mutate(
    SBP_mean   = rowMeans(across(c(BPXOSY1, BPXOSY2, BPXOSY3)), na.rm = TRUE),
    DBP_mean   = rowMeans(across(c(BPXODI1, BPXODI2, BPXODI3)), na.rm = TRUE),
    PULSE_mean = rowMeans(across(c(BPXOPLS1, BPXOPLS2, BPXOPLS3)), na.rm = TRUE),
    across(c(SBP_mean, DBP_mean, PULSE_mean), ~ if_else(is.nan(.x), NA_real_, .x)),
    FAST_HOURS = PHAFSTHR + PHAFSTMN / 60,
    # serum cotinine >= 3 ng/mL indicates active tobacco use (Benowitz et al., 2009)
    SMOKER_COT = factor(if_else(LBXCOT >= 3, "yes", "no"), levels = c("no", "yes"))
  )

bp_readings <- c(paste0("BPXOSY", 1:3), paste0("BPXODI", 1:3), paste0("BPXOPLS", 1:3))
derived_labels <- tribble(
  ~variable,    ~label,
  "SBP_mean",   "Systolic blood pressure, mean of readings (mmHg)",
  "DBP_mean",   "Diastolic blood pressure, mean of readings (mmHg)",
  "PULSE_mean", "Pulse, mean of readings (/min)",
  "FAST_HOURS", "Fasting time before blood draw (hours)",
  "SMOKER_COT", "Active tobacco use (serum cotinine >= 3 ng/mL)")

nhanes <- nhanes %>%
  select(-all_of(c(dup_unit_vars, lod_removed, setdiff(constant_vars, "SDDSRVYR"),
                   bp_readings, lod_codes)))

log_step("Redundant columns", nhanes,
         paste0("Removed ", length(dup_unit_vars), " unit duplicates, ", length(lod_removed),
                " analytes with >", MAX_BELOW_LOD * 100, "% below LOD, ", length(lod_codes),
                " LOD comment codes, constant columns and the 9 single BP readings (replaced by their means). ",
                "Added derived variables SBP_mean, DBP_mean, PULSE_mean, FAST_HOURS, SMOKER_COT."))
```

# Missing values

## How much is missing?

```{r missing-overview, fig.height = 4}
missing_per_variable <- tibble(variable = names(nhanes),
                               missing = map_dbl(nhanes, ~ mean(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  left_join(variable_overview %>% select(variable, label, file, component), by = "variable") %>%
  mutate(component = replace_na(component, "Derived"))

summary(missing_per_variable$missing)

missing_per_variable %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = missing * 100, fill = component)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "% of participants with a missing value", y = "number of variables",
       title = "Missingness per variable (all participants)")
```

Only a handful of variables are complete; most variables are missing for 30–60% of the participants. This is
far too much to be random noise, so we look for the mechanism behind it.

## Where and why are values missing?

NHANES has a nested design that explains most of the missing values:

1. **Interview only.** `RIDSTATR` = 1 means that the participant was interviewed but did not visit the mobile
   examination centre. These participants have no examination or laboratory data at all.
2. **Eligibility by age and sex.** Many measurements are only done in certain age groups (e.g. glycohemoglobin
   from 12 years on, the alcohol questionnaire from 18 on, early childhood questions up to 15 years) or only in
   women/young children (ferritin, transferrin receptor, pregnancy test).
3. **Random subsamples by design.** Fasting measurements (glucose, insulin, triglycerides, LDL) are only done
   in the morning session, and PFAS and volatile organic compounds in a random one-third subsample.
4. **Item non-response.** Refusals, failed blood draws or insufficient sample volume.

The heatmap below shows, for a random selection of 1500 participants, which values are observed. Rows are
split by examination status and age group, columns by NHANES component.

```{r missing-heatmap, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7}
age_groups <- function(age) cut(age, breaks = c(-Inf, 11, 19, 39, 59, Inf),
                                labels = c("0-11", "12-19", "20-39", "40-59", "60-80"))

heatmap_rows <- nhanes %>%
  mutate(status = if_else(RIDSTATR == 2, "examined", "interview only"),
         age_group = age_groups(RIDAGEYR)) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 1500)

heatmap_vars <- missing_per_variable %>%
  filter(!variable %in% c("SEQN", weights_design), component != "Derived") %>%
  arrange(component, file)

observed_matrix <- heatmap_rows %>%
  select(all_of(heatmap_vars$variable)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ as.numeric(!is.na(.x)))) %>%
  as.matrix()

Heatmap(observed_matrix,
        name = "value",
        col = c("0" = "grey92", "1" = "#2C5F8A"),
        heatmap_legend_param = list(labels = c("missing", "observed"), at = c(0, 1)),
        row_split = paste(heatmap_rows$status, heatmap_rows$age_group, sep = ", "),
        column_split = heatmap_vars$component,
        cluster_rows = FALSE, cluster_columns = FALSE,
        cluster_row_slices = FALSE, cluster_column_slices = FALSE,
        show_row_names = FALSE, show_column_names = FALSE,
        row_title_rot = 0, row_title_gp = gpar(fontsize = 8),
        column_title_gp = gpar(fontsize = 8), column_title_rot = 90,
        use_raster = TRUE)
```

The same information summarised per data file and age group:

```{r missing-by-file-age, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 8}
nhanes %>%
  mutate(age_group = age_groups(RIDAGEYR),
         status = if_else(RIDSTATR == 2, "examined", "interview only")) %>%
  select(SEQN, status, age_group, all_of(heatmap_vars$variable)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(SEQN, status, age_group), names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value", values_transform = as.character) %>%
  left_join(variable_overview %>% select(variable, file), by = "variable") %>%
  group_by(status, age_group, file) %>%
  summarise(observed = mean(!is.na(value)) * 100, .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = fct_rev(file), fill = observed)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(observed)), size = 2.3) +
  facet_wrap(~status) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1, limits = c(0, 100)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "age group (years)", y = "NHANES data file", fill = "% observed",
       title = "Missingness is largely structural: examination status and age decide what is measured")
```

```{r fasting-by-design}
# fasting labs are only measured in the morning session
nhanes %>%
  filter(RIDSTATR == 2, RIDAGEYR >= 12) %>%
  group_by(session = factor(PHDSESNZ, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("morning", "afternoon/evening"))) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), fasting_glucose_measured = mean(!is.na(LBXGLU)),
            HbA1c_measured = mean(!is.na(LBXGH)))
```

**Is the remaining missingness random?** Among examined adults, a missing blood sample is not the result of the
design. We check whether participants with and without a glycohemoglobin result (a measurement that should be
available for all examined adults) differ in age, sex and income, using the tests from the statistics
practical.

```{r missing-not-random}
missing_check <- nhanes %>%
  filter(RIDSTATR == 2, RIDAGEYR >= MIN_AGE) %>%
  mutate(HbA1c_missing = factor(is.na(LBXGH), labels = c("observed", "missing")))

table(missing_check$HbA1c_missing)
wilcox.test(RIDAGEYR ~ HbA1c_missing, data = missing_check)
chisq.test(table(missing_check$RIAGENDR, missing_check$HbA1c_missing))
wilcox.test(INDFMPIR ~ HbA1c_missing, data = missing_check)

missing_summary <- missing_check %>%
  group_by(HbA1c_missing) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), median_age = median(RIDAGEYR), pct_female = mean(RIAGENDR == 2) * 100,
            median_income_ratio = median(INDFMPIR, na.rm = TRUE))
missing_summary
```

Only `r round(mean(missing_check$HbA1c_missing == "missing") * 100, 1)`% of the examined adults lack a blood
result. Sex does not differ between both groups, but participants without a blood result have a lower
income-to-poverty ratio (median `r round(missing_summary$median_income_ratio[2], 2)` versus
`r round(missing_summary$median_income_ratio[1], 2)`) and are slightly younger. The missingness is therefore
**not completely at random**: it depends on observed characteristics (missing at random with respect to income
and age). Because the fraction is small, the impact is limited, but it is reported as a possible source of bias.

**How do we handle missingness?**

* Structural missingness (not examined, not eligible) is handled by restricting the **analysis population**
  (next section) instead of by imputation: imputing a pregnancy test for men or an alcohol questionnaire for
  children makes no sense.
* Subsample missingness (fasting labs, PFAS, VOCs) is missing completely at random *within* the eligible
  group, but only by design. Fasting variables can be used, but analyses with them are automatically restricted
  to the morning-session subsample (about half of the participants).
* The small amount of item non-response that remains is **not imputed** in the exported dataset. Each analysis
  in Parts 2–3 uses complete cases on the variables it needs, which is the most transparent choice. Where an
  algorithm needs a complete matrix (PCA in this notebook, machine learning in Part 4), the choice (complete
  cases or imputation fitted on the training data only) is made and reported in that analysis.

# Analysis population and feature filtering

## Samples

Based on the missingness structure, the analysis population is defined as:

* **examined participants** (`RIDSTATR` = 2): only they have examination and laboratory data;
* **adults aged `r MIN_AGE` or older**: most laboratory panels, the education variable and the alcohol
  questionnaire are adult measurements, and adult reference values differ from those in children;
* **not pregnant** (`RIDEXPRG` = 1 or a positive urine pregnancy test): pregnancy changes many laboratory values
  (e.g. haemoglobin, lipids, hormones) and the group is too small (n ≈ 40) to study separately.

```{r sample-selection}
flow <- tibble(step = "All participants", n = nrow(nhanes))

analysis <- nhanes %>% filter(RIDSTATR == 2)
flow <- add_row(flow, step = "Examined in the mobile examination centre", n = nrow(analysis))

analysis <- analysis %>% filter(RIDAGEYR >= MIN_AGE)
flow <- add_row(flow, step = paste0("Aged ", MIN_AGE, " years or older"), n = nrow(analysis))

analysis <- analysis %>% filter(!(RIDEXPRG %in% 1), !(URXPREG %in% 1))
flow <- add_row(flow, step = "Not pregnant", n = nrow(analysis))

knitr::kable(flow, caption = "Participant flow")
log_step("Analysis population", analysis,
         paste0("Kept examined participants (RIDSTATR = 2) aged >= ", MIN_AGE, " who are not pregnant."))
```

## Features

Within this population, features that are mostly missing cannot support any analysis. We remove features missing
in more than `r MAX_MISSING_FEATURE * 100`% of the analysis population. With this threshold the fasting
subsample (about 50% observed) is kept, while the PFAS and VOC subsamples (about one third) and the
children/women-only measurements are removed. Next, near-zero-variance features (one value in more than
`r NZV_THRESHOLD * 100`% of the observations) are removed.

```{r feature-filter}
metadata_vars <- c("SEQN", weights_design, technical, "FAST_HOURS")
candidate_features <- setdiff(names(analysis), metadata_vars)

feature_missing <- tibble(variable = candidate_features,
                          missing = map_dbl(candidate_features, ~ mean(is.na(analysis[[.x]])))) %>%
  left_join(missing_per_variable %>% select(variable, label, component), by = "variable")

feature_missing %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(variable, missing), y = missing * 100,
             fill = missing > MAX_MISSING_FEATURE)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = MAX_MISSING_FEATURE * 100, linetype = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey60", "#C95C4F"), labels = c("kept", "removed")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = c(0, 100)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(), axis.line.x = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "features (ordered by missingness)", y = "% missing in analysis population", fill = "",
       title = "Feature filtering on missingness")

too_missing <- feature_missing %>% filter(missing > MAX_MISSING_FEATURE) %>% pull(variable)

top_share <- function(x) { x <- na.omit(x); if (length(x) == 0) return(1); max(table(x)) / length(x) }
near_zero_var <- tibble(variable = setdiff(candidate_features, too_missing)) %>%
  mutate(top_value_share = map_dbl(variable, ~ top_share(analysis[[.x]]))) %>%
  filter(top_value_share > NZV_THRESHOLD) %>%
  left_join(missing_per_variable %>% select(variable, label), by = "variable")
near_zero_var

analysis <- analysis %>% select(-all_of(c(too_missing, near_zero_var$variable)))
features <- setdiff(names(analysis), metadata_vars)

log_step("Feature filtering", analysis,
         paste0("Removed ", length(too_missing), " features with >", MAX_MISSING_FEATURE * 100,
                "% missing and ", nrow(near_zero_var), " near-zero-variance features (top value >",
                NZV_THRESHOLD * 100, "%)."))
length(features)
```

After filtering, `r length(features)` features remain for `r nrow(analysis)` participants.

## Categorical variables as factors

The remaining categorical codes are converted to factors. The most important demographic variables get
readable labels.

```{r factors}
analysis <- analysis %>%
  mutate(
    RIAGENDR = factor(RIAGENDR, levels = 1:2, labels = c("male", "female")),
    RIDRETH3 = factor(RIDRETH3, levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7),
                      labels = c("Mexican American", "Other Hispanic", "Non-Hispanic White",
                                 "Non-Hispanic Black", "Non-Hispanic Asian", "Other/multiracial")),
    DMDEDUC2 = factor(DMDEDUC2, levels = 1:5, ordered = TRUE,
                      labels = c("< 9th grade", "9-11th grade", "high school/GED",
                                 "some college/AA", "college graduate+")),
    DMDMARTZ = factor(DMDMARTZ, levels = 1:3,
                      labels = c("married/living with partner", "widowed/divorced/separated",
                                 "never married")),
    DMDBORN4 = factor(DMDBORN4, levels = 1:2, labels = c("USA", "other country")),
    RIDEXMON = factor(RIDEXMON, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Nov-Apr", "May-Oct")),
    PHDSESNZ = factor(PHDSESNZ, levels = 0:1, labels = c("morning", "afternoon/evening")),
    across(any_of(c("DMQMILIZ", "ALQ111", "ALQ151")),
           ~ factor(.x, levels = 1:2, labels = c("yes", "no"))),
    across(any_of(setdiff(nominal, c("RIAGENDR", "RIDRETH3", "DMDMARTZ", "DMDBORN4",
                                     "DMQMILIZ", "ALQ111", "ALQ151"))), as.factor),
    across(any_of(setdiff(ordinal, "DMDEDUC2")), ~ factor(.x, ordered = TRUE))
  )

# RIDRETH1 is a coarser version of RIDRETH3 (Asian participants are pooled with "other"): keep RIDRETH3
analysis <- analysis %>% select(-any_of("RIDRETH1"))
features <- setdiff(features, "RIDRETH1")

continuous_features <- features[map_lgl(features, ~ is.numeric(analysis[[.x]]) &&
                                          n_distinct(na.omit(analysis[[.x]])) > 15)]
length(continuous_features)
```

# Implausible values and outliers

## Biologically impossible values

For key clinical variables we define generous plausibility limits. Values outside these limits would point to
measurement or data-entry errors and are set to missing.

```{r plausibility}
plausibility <- tribble(
  ~variable,    ~lower, ~upper,
  "SBP_mean",       60,    270,
  "DBP_mean",       25,    160,
  "PULSE_mean",     30,    200,
  "BMXHT",         120,    220,
  "BMXWT",          25,    300,
  "BMXBMI",         12,     90,
  "BMXWAIST",       40,    200,
  "LBXGH",           3,     20,
  "LBXGLU",         30,    700,
  "LBXTC",          50,    700,
  "LBDHDD",          5,    200,
  "LBXHGB",          4,     22) %>%
  filter(variable %in% names(analysis)) %>%
  mutate(n_below = map2_int(variable, lower, ~ sum(analysis[[.x]] < .y, na.rm = TRUE)),
         n_above = map2_int(variable, upper, ~ sum(analysis[[.x]] > .y, na.rm = TRUE)),
         observed_min = map_dbl(variable, ~ min(analysis[[.x]], na.rm = TRUE)),
         observed_max = map_dbl(variable, ~ max(analysis[[.x]], na.rm = TRUE)))
knitr::kable(plausibility, caption = "Plausibility check of key clinical variables")

for (i in seq_len(nrow(plausibility))) {
  v <- plausibility$variable[i]
  out <- analysis[[v]] < plausibility$lower[i] | analysis[[v]] > plausibility$upper[i]
  analysis[[v]][which(out)] <- NA
}
```

Values outside the plausible range are rare or absent: the dataset has already been cleaned by NHANES.
Extreme but possible values (e.g. a glucose of 500 mg/dL in an untreated diabetic) are **not** removed.

## Distributions and transformation

Many laboratory values are right-skewed (concentrations cannot be negative, and a few participants have very
high values, e.g. CRP during an infection or cotinine in smokers). Skewed variables violate the assumptions of
the linear models and t-tests of Parts 2–3 and dominate distance-based methods such as PCA. Continuous features
with a skewness above `r SKEW_THRESHOLD` are therefore **log2-transformed** (one unit = a doubling). Variables
with zeros get a small offset (half of the smallest positive value).

```{r skewness}
skew_table <- tibble(variable = continuous_features) %>%
  mutate(skew_raw  = map_dbl(variable, ~ skewness(analysis[[.x]])),
         min_value = map_dbl(variable, ~ min(analysis[[.x]], na.rm = TRUE)),
         transform = skew_raw > SKEW_THRESHOLD & min_value >= 0)

log_vars <- skew_table %>% filter(transform) %>% pull(variable)

analysis_transformed <- analysis
offsets <- c()
for (v in log_vars) {
  x <- analysis[[v]]
  offset <- if (min(x, na.rm = TRUE) == 0) min(x[x > 0], na.rm = TRUE) / 2 else 0
  offsets[v] <- offset
  analysis_transformed[[v]] <- log2(x + offset)
}

skew_table <- skew_table %>%
  mutate(skew_after = map_dbl(variable, ~ skewness(analysis_transformed[[.x]])))

skew_table %>%
  pivot_longer(c(skew_raw, skew_after), names_to = "version", values_to = "skewness") %>%
  mutate(version = factor(version, levels = c("skew_raw", "skew_after"),
                          labels = c("before transformation", "after transformation"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = skewness)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "grey40", boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-SKEW_THRESHOLD, SKEW_THRESHOLD), linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~version, ncol = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-5, 30)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "skewness", y = "number of features",
       title = paste0(length(log_vars), " of ", length(continuous_features),
                      " continuous features were log2-transformed"))

log_step("Transformation", analysis_transformed,
         paste0("log2-transformed ", length(log_vars), " right-skewed continuous features (skewness > ",
                SKEW_THRESHOLD, "); offset = half the smallest positive value when zeros were present."))
```

```{r transformation-examples, fig.height = 5}
example_vars <- c(LBXHSCRP = "CRP (mg/L)", LBXCOT = "cotinine (ng/mL)",
                  LBXTLG = "triglycerides (mg/dL)", LBXSATSI = "ALT (IU/L)")
example_vars <- example_vars[names(example_vars) %in% log_vars]

bind_rows(
  analysis %>% select(all_of(names(example_vars))) %>% mutate(version = "original scale"),
  analysis_transformed %>% select(all_of(names(example_vars))) %>% mutate(version = "log2 scale")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-version, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(version = fct_relevel(version, "original scale"),
         variable = example_vars[variable]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#2C5F8A", colour = "#2C5F8A", alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(version ~ variable, scales = "free") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "", y = "density", title = "Examples of skewed laboratory values before and after log2 transformation")
```

Cotinine stays bimodal after transformation: non-smokers have values near the detection limit and smokers
values that are about 1000 times higher. This is biology, not a technical artefact, and it is the reason why
the derived variable `SMOKER_COT` is useful.

## Outlying values and participants

After transformation, we flag values more than `r ROBUST_Z` robust standard deviations
(median ± `r ROBUST_Z` × 1.4826 × MAD) from the median. Robust statistics are used because the mean and SD
themselves are influenced by outliers. Cotinine and hydroxycotinine are left out of this count: their
distribution is bimodal (smokers versus non-smokers), so every smoker would be flagged as an outlier.

```{r outliers}
robust_z <- function(x) (x - median(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / (1.4826 * mad(x, na.rm = TRUE, constant = 1))
outlier_features <- setdiff(continuous_features, c("LBXCOT", "LBXHCOT"))

z_matrix <- analysis_transformed %>%
  select(all_of(outlier_features)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), robust_z)) %>%
  as.matrix()
z_matrix[!is.finite(z_matrix)] <- NA     # features with MAD = 0

outlier_per_feature <- tibble(variable = outlier_features,
                              n_outliers = colSums(abs(z_matrix) > ROBUST_Z, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  left_join(variable_overview %>% select(variable, label), by = "variable") %>%
  arrange(desc(n_outliers))
head(outlier_per_feature, 10)

outlier_per_sample <- tibble(SEQN = analysis_transformed$SEQN,
                             n_outlying = rowSums(abs(z_matrix) > ROBUST_Z, na.rm = TRUE),
                             n_measured = rowSums(!is.na(z_matrix))) %>%
  mutate(pct_outlying = n_outlying / n_measured * 100)
```

```{r outliers-plot, fig.height = 3.5}
outlier_per_sample %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n_outlying)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey40") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = paste0("number of features with |robust z| > ", ROBUST_Z), y = "number of participants",
       title = "Most participants have no or very few outlying values")
```

```{r outliers-inspect}
# which features are outlying in the participants with the most outliers?
top_outlier_samples <- outlier_per_sample %>% slice_max(n_outlying, n = 5)
for (s in top_outlier_samples$SEQN) {
  i <- which(analysis_transformed$SEQN == s)
  flagged <- outlier_features[which(abs(z_matrix[i, ]) > ROBUST_Z)]
  cat("SEQN", s, "- age", analysis_transformed$RIDAGEYR[i], "-",
      as.character(analysis_transformed$RIAGENDR[i]), ":",
      paste(flagged, collapse = ", "), "\n")
}
```

**Interpretation.** Outlying values cluster in features where extreme values are clinically meaningful
(glucose and HbA1c in diabetes, the albumin–creatinine ratio in kidney disease, progesterone in the luteal phase
or pregnancy-like hormonal states, sodium disturbances). Participants with many outlying values show a coherent,
disease-like profile rather than random errors, e.g. a kidney profile (albumin–creatinine ratio, creatinine,
phosphorus, potassium, blood pressure), a diabetic profile (glucose, HbA1c, triglycerides, urinary albumin) or
an anaemia/haemolysis-like profile (haemoglobin, haematocrit, RDW, LDH, bilirubin).
We therefore consider them **interesting biology and keep them**; they are flagged in the exported dataset
(`n_outlying_features`) so that sensitivity analyses without them remain possible. Robust methods or
transformations are preferred over removing participants.

# Quality control: correlation structure and PCA

## Correlation between laboratory features

If the preprocessing is correct, features that measure related physiology should correlate. For the laboratory
features we calculate Spearman correlations (pairwise complete observations) and cluster them.

```{r correlation-heatmap, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 10}
lab_features <- intersect(continuous_features,
                          variable_overview %>% filter(component == "Laboratory") %>% pull(variable))

cor_matrix <- cor(analysis_transformed[, lab_features], use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")
lab_labels <- variable_overview$label[match(lab_features, variable_overview$variable)]
dimnames(cor_matrix) <- list(str_trunc(lab_labels, 30), str_trunc(lab_labels, 30))

Heatmap(cor_matrix,
        name = "Spearman\nrho",
        col = colorRamp2(c(-1, 0, 1), c("#2166AC", "white", "#B2182B")),
        clustering_distance_rows = function(m) as.dist(1 - abs(cor(t(m)))),
        clustering_distance_columns = function(m) as.dist(1 - abs(cor(t(m)))),
        row_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 4), column_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 4),
        show_row_dend = FALSE,
        column_title = "Correlation structure of the laboratory features")
```

The expected blocks appear (e.g. the lipid panel, red blood cell indices, white blood cell counts, folate forms,
fatty acids, sex hormones, liver enzymes), which supports that the data are consistent. Very strongly correlated
pairs (e.g. haemoglobin and haematocrit, total and serum cholesterol from two different labs) are a reminder to
check for **multicollinearity** before putting such features together in a regression model (Part 2).

## Principal component analysis

Do participants group by biology or by a technical factor? PCA is run on the laboratory features with at most
`r PCA_MAX_MISSING * 100`% missing (fasting measurements are thereby excluded, as they would restrict the PCA to
the morning session). Participants with complete data on these features are used, and all features are
standardised (z-scores) so that each contributes equally.

```{r pca}
pca_features <- lab_features[map_dbl(lab_features, ~ mean(is.na(analysis_transformed[[.x]]))) <= PCA_MAX_MISSING]

pca_input <- analysis_transformed %>%
  select(SEQN, all_of(pca_features)) %>%
  drop_na()
c(n_features = length(pca_features), n_participants = nrow(pca_input))

pca_res <- prcomp(pca_input %>% select(-SEQN), center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

pca_scores <- as_tibble(pca_res$x[, 1:10]) %>%
  mutate(SEQN = pca_input$SEQN) %>%
  left_join(analysis_transformed %>%
              select(SEQN, RIAGENDR, RIDAGEYR, RIDRETH3, BMXBMI, SMOKER_COT, INDFMPIR, DMDEDUC2,
                     PHDSESNZ, RIDEXMON, FAST_HOURS, SDMVPSU, SDMVSTRA),
            by = "SEQN") %>%
  mutate(age_group = age_groups(RIDAGEYR))
```

```{r pca-scree, fig.height = 3.5}
explained <- tibble(PC = seq_along(pca_res$sdev), variance = pca_res$sdev^2 / sum(pca_res$sdev^2) * 100)

explained %>%
  filter(PC <= 20) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PC, y = variance)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey60") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), breaks = 1:20) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "principal component", y = "% of variance explained",
       title = "Variance explained by the first 20 principal components")
```

```{r pca-plots, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7.5}
pc_lab <- function(k) paste0("PC", k, " (", round(explained$variance[k], 1), "%)")

pca_plot <- function(colour_var, title) {
  pca_scores %>%
    drop_na(all_of(colour_var)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = .data[[colour_var]])) +
    geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
    scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) +
    theme_classic() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    labs(x = pc_lab(1), y = pc_lab(2), colour = "", title = title)
}

pca_plots <- list(pca_plot("RIAGENDR",  "sex (biological)"),
                  pca_plot("age_group", "age group (biological)"),
                  pca_plot("PHDSESNZ",  "exam session (technical)"),
                  pca_plot("RIDEXMON",  "six-month period (technical)"))

# arrange the four plots in a 2 x 2 grid (base grid, no extra packages needed)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(2, 2)))
for (k in seq_along(pca_plots)) {
  print(pca_plots[[k]], vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = (k - 1) %/% 2 + 1,
                                      layout.pos.col = (k - 1) %% 2 + 1))
}
```

To quantify what drives each component, every PC is regressed on one covariate at a time; the R² (% of the PC's
variance explained by that covariate) is shown in a heatmap.

```{r pca-covariates, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5}
covariates <- c(sex = "RIAGENDR", age = "RIDAGEYR", `ethnicity` = "RIDRETH3", BMI = "BMXBMI",
                `smoking (cotinine)` = "SMOKER_COT", `income/poverty ratio` = "INDFMPIR",
                education = "DMDEDUC2", `exam session` = "PHDSESNZ", `six-month period` = "RIDEXMON",
                `fasting time` = "FAST_HOURS", `pseudo-PSU` = "SDMVPSU", `pseudo-stratum` = "SDMVSTRA")
covariate_kind <- c(rep("biological", 7), rep("technical / design", 5))

r2_matrix <- sapply(paste0("PC", 1:10), function(pc) {
  sapply(covariates, function(cv) {
    d <- pca_scores %>% transmute(y = .data[[pc]], x = .data[[cv]]) %>% drop_na()
    if (cv == "SDMVSTRA") d$x <- factor(d$x)              # stratum is a category, not a number
    if (is.ordered(d$x)) d$x <- factor(d$x, ordered = FALSE)
    summary(lm(y ~ x, data = d))$r.squared * 100
  })
})

Heatmap(r2_matrix,
        name = "R2 (%)",
        col = colorRamp2(c(0, max(r2_matrix)), c("white", "#B2182B")),
        cluster_rows = FALSE, cluster_columns = FALSE,
        row_split = covariate_kind, row_title_rot = 0,
        column_names_rot = 0, column_names_centered = TRUE,
        cell_fun = function(j, i, x, y, width, height, fill) {
          grid.text(sprintf("%.0f", r2_matrix[i, j]), x, y, gp = gpar(fontsize = 7))
        },
        column_title = "% of variance of each principal component explained by a covariate")
```

```{r pca-loadings, fig.height = 5}
loading_labels <- variable_overview$label[match(rownames(pca_res$rotation), variable_overview$variable)]

as_tibble(pca_res$rotation[, 1:2]) %>%
  mutate(feature = str_trunc(loading_labels, 40)) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(PC1, PC2), names_to = "PC", values_to = "loading") %>%
  group_by(PC) %>%
  slice_max(abs(loading), n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(feature, abs(loading)), y = loading, fill = loading > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~PC, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2166AC", "#B2182B"), guide = "none") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7)) +
  labs(x = "", y = "loading", title = "Features with the largest loadings on PC1 and PC2")
```

**Interpretation.** No distinct clusters appear: the participants form one continuous cloud, as expected for
a population sample. The main axes of variation are biological: PC1 is driven mostly by age, PC2 by sex (sex
hormones, haemoglobin/red cell indices, creatinine) and PC3 by BMI, while the later components also pick up
ethnicity and smoking. The technical factors exam session, six-month period and fasting time explain almost
none of the variance (R² ≤ 2%). The pseudo-strata explain a few percent, which is expected because they
reflect geography and therefore the ethnic and socio-economic make-up of the sampled areas. The participants
therefore group by the biology we care about rather than by a technical batch. Because the fasting measurements only exist for the morning session, `PHDSESNZ` should still be kept in
mind as a design factor whenever fasting variables are analysed. The six-month period is confounded with
geography (the mobile examination centres visit warmer locations in winter), so a small association with it is
not necessarily a technical artefact.

# Export the preprocessed dataset

The exported dataset contains, for each participant of the analysis population:

* `SEQN` and the survey weights/design variables (metadata, not features);
* technical variables (exam session, six-month period, fasting time) as possible covariates;
* all retained features, with skewed continuous features on the **log2 scale** (column names are unchanged,
  the dictionary indicates which ones were transformed);
* the number of outlying features per participant (`n_outlying_features`).

Missing values are **not** imputed. Features are **not** standardised in the exported file (to keep effect sizes
interpretable); standardisation is done within each multivariate analysis.

```{r export}
final <- analysis_transformed %>%
  left_join(outlier_per_sample %>% select(SEQN, n_outlying_features = n_outlying), by = "SEQN") %>%
  select(SEQN, all_of(intersect(weights_design, names(.))), any_of(technical), FAST_HOURS,
         all_of(features), n_outlying_features)

variable_dictionary <- tibble(variable = names(final)) %>%
  left_join(bind_rows(variable_overview %>% select(variable, label, file, component, type),
                      derived_labels %>% mutate(component = "Derived", type = "derived")),
            by = "variable") %>%
  mutate(role = case_when(variable == "SEQN" ~ "identifier",
                          variable %in% weights_design ~ "survey weight / design",
                          variable %in% c(technical, "FAST_HOURS") ~ "technical covariate",
                          variable == "n_outlying_features" ~ "QC flag",
                          TRUE ~ "feature"),
         class = map_chr(variable, ~ class(final[[.x]])[1]),
         transformation = case_when(!variable %in% log_vars ~ "none",
                                    offsets[variable] == 0 ~ "log2(x)",
                                    TRUE ~ paste0("log2(x + ", signif(offsets[variable], 3), ")")),
         pct_missing = map_dbl(variable, ~ round(mean(is.na(final[[.x]])) * 100, 1)))

log_step("Final dataset", final, "Exported preprocessed dataset (no imputation, no scaling).")

dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(final, "output/NHANES_part1_preprocessed.csv")
saveRDS(final, "output/NHANES_part1_preprocessed.rds")   # keeps factor levels
write_csv(variable_dictionary, "output/NHANES_part1_variable_dictionary.csv")
write_csv(preprocessing_log, "output/NHANES_part1_preprocessing_log.csv")

knitr::kable(preprocessing_log, caption = "Preprocessing log")

variable_dictionary %>%
  filter(role == "feature") %>%
  count(component, transformation = transformation != "none") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = transformation, values_from = n, values_fill = 0,
              names_prefix = "log2_transformed_") %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Retained features per component")
```

# Is the dataset suitable for Parts 2–4?

* **Sample size.** About `r format(nrow(final), big.mark = " ")` adults with `r length(features)` features is
  ample for multivariable regression (Part 2), for testing many features (Part 3) and for training and testing
  a prediction model (Part 4).
* **Outcome and covariates.** Typical confounders are available and mostly complete: age, sex, ethnicity,
  BMI, income-to-poverty ratio, education and smoking status (cotinine).
* **Fasting variables** are only available for about half of the participants (morning session); questions on
  insulin resistance or LDL must use this subsample and report its size.
* **Transformations.** Coefficients of log2-transformed variables are interpreted per doubling of the value.
* **Limitations to report:** unweighted analysis of a complex survey; top-coded age (80+) and income ratio (5+);
  values below the detection limit replaced by LOD/√2 by NHANES; possible non-random missingness of the blood
  sample; cross-sectional data, so associations are not causal.
